A Stochastic Riemannian Alternating Descent Ascent Method for Nonsmooth Composite Expectation Optimization on Riemannian ManifoldsThanks: Submitted to the editors DATE.

Meng Xu ††thanks: ICMSEC, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China. (). Email: xumeng22@mails.ucas.ac.cn    Bo Jiang ††thanks: Ministry of Education Key Laboratory of NSLSCS, School of Mathematical Sciences, Nanjing Normal University, Nanjing, China (). Email: jiangbo@njnu.edu.cn    Ya-Feng Liu ††thanks: Ministry of Education Key Laboratory of Mathematics and Information Networks, School of Mathematical Sciences, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, China. (). Email: yafengliu@bupt.edu.cn    Anthony Man-Cho So ††thanks: Department of Systems Engineering and Engineering Management, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, HKSAR, China. (). Abstract

In this paper, we consider a class of Riemannian nonsmooth composite expectation optimization problems, which arises in various machine learning, signal processing, and statistics applications. Noting that these problems admit structured minimax reformulations, we propose an efficient algorithm, named stochastic Riemannian alternating descent ascent method with recursive momentum (StoRADA-RM), to tackle them. StoRADA-RM performs one or multiple Riemannian stochastic gradient descent steps and then a proximal gradient ascent step at each iteration. To compute the Riemannian stochastic gradient, we propose a vector transport-free recursive momentum estimator that requires only 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) stochastic gradient evaluations per iteration. We prove that StoRADA-RM returns an ϵ\epsilon-Riemannian-stochastic-stationary point of a given problem in the said class in 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) iterations while making 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) calls to a stochastic first-order oracle (SFO). Both the iteration complexity and SFO complexity bounds are the best known in the literature for the said class of problems. The latter even matches the optimal lower bound for smooth nonconvex optimization with stochastic first-order algorithms. We then present numerical results on sparse principal component analysis and coordinate-independent sparse estimation to demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed method.

keywords
Riemannian nonsmooth optimization, Riemannian alternating descent ascent method, stochastic gradient descent, stochastic first-order oracle complexity, sparse principal component analysis.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we consider Riemannian nonsmooth expectation optimization problems of the form

minx∈ℳ{Φ(x):=f(x)+h(𝒜(x))},f(x):=𝔼ω∼𝒟[f(x;ω)],\min_{x\in\mathcal{M}}\left\{\Phi(x):=f(x)+h(\mathcal{A}(x))\right\},\quad f(x):=\mathbb{E}_{\omega\sim\mathcal{D}}[f(x;\omega)], (1.1)

where ω\omega is a random vector with probability distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, ℳ\mathcal{M} is a Riemannian manifold embedded in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space ℰ1\mathcal{E}_{1}, f⁡(⋅,θ):ℰ1→ℝf(\cdot;\theta):\mathcal{E}_{1}\to\mathbb{R} is a continuously differentiable function for each θ\theta in the range of ω\omega, h:ℰ2→ℝh:\mathcal{E}_{2}\to\mathbb{R} with ℰ2\mathcal{E}_{2} being another finite-dimensional Euclidean space is a convex and LhL_{h}-Lipschitz continuous function, and 𝒜:ℰ1→ℰ2\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{E}_{1}\to\mathcal{E}_{2} is a smooth map. When the range of ω\omega is finite and given by {θ1,θ2,…,θN}\{\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\ldots,\theta_{N}\}, and ω\omega has the uniform distribution, the function ff reduces to the finite-sum form f⁡(x)=1N​∑i=1Nf⁡(x,θi)f(x)=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(x;\theta_{i}). Many applications in machine learning, signal processing, and statistics give rise to instances of problem (1.1), such as sparse principal component analysis (PCA) [52, 24], coordinate-independent sparse estimation (CISE) [11, 42], and robust low rank matrix completion [20].

A variety of deterministic algorithms can be applied to solve problem (1.1) in the finite-sum setting, including Riemannian subgradient-type methods [6, 18, 17, 30, 19], Riemannian proximal gradient-type methods [9, 21, 22, 41, 10, 31], Riemannian smoothing-type algorithms [3, 33, 47], Riemannian splitting-type methods [27, 26, 15, 29, 51, 13, 43], and Riemannian minimax algorithms [45, 44]. Despite the growing interest in developing stochastic algorithms for tackling problem (1.1), existing works on this topic remain limited. In this paper, we focus on the case where the full gradient of ff is inaccessible as in the online setting, or intractable due to the extremely large number of component functions as in the finite-sum setting. Our goal is to develop an efficient stochastic algorithm for tackling problem (1.1).

1.1 Related Works

When the nonsmooth term h≡0h\equiv 0, problem (1.1) reduces to a smooth expectation optimization problem. A typical method for tackling such a problem is Riemannian stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [5], which is an extension of the classical Euclidean SGD method for the manifold setting. To further improve practical performance and theoretical guarantees, variance reduction techniques have been extensively studied in both Euclidean and Riemannian settings. Notable Riemannian stochastic algorithms with variance reduction include Riemannian stochastic variance-reduced gradient (RSVRG) methods [48, 23, 37], the Riemannian stochastic recursive gradient (RSRG) method [25], Riemannian stochastic path-integrated differential estimator (RSPIDER) methods [49, 50], and the Riemannian stochastic recursive momentum (RSTORM) method [16]. It should be noted that RSVRG and RSRG are designed for finite-sum minimization problems, and they require computing the full gradient once in every fixed number of iterations. As such, they are not applicable to the setting of our interest, where full gradients are inaccessible. Although RSPIDER can avoid computing the full gradient and achieve the optimal 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexity for finding an ϵ\epsilon-Riemannian-stochastic-stationary (ϵ\epsilon-RSS) point of problem (1.1), it still needs to compute a large-batch gradient of size 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) in each epoch and a mini-batch size of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}) at each inner iteration. To address these limitations, Han and Gao [16] proposed RSTORM, which only requires 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) stochastic gradient evaluations per iteration and avoids computing full or large-batch gradients. They further established that RSTORM achieves a near-optimal 𝒪~​(ϵ−3)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}) SFO complexity for finding ϵ\epsilon-RSS points of smooth expectation optimization problems on Riemannian manifolds.11 1 Here and in what follows, we use 𝒪~​(⋅)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot) to hide poly-logarithmic factors.

When the nonsmooth term h≠0h\not=0, various efforts on developing stochastic algorithms for tackling problem (1.1) have focused on the Euclidean setting, where ℳ⊆ℰ1\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{1} is a closed convex set. Of particular interest are stochastic proximal gradient methods with variance-reduced gradient estimators, which are motivated by the success of variance reduction techniques in improving both numerical performance and SFO complexity. Specifically, when ℳ=ℰ1\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{E}_{1} and 𝒜=ℐ\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{I} with ℐ\mathcal{I} being the identity map, Pham et al. proposed Prox-SARAH [34] and Wang et al. proposed SpiderBoost [40], both achieving an SFO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) for finding an ϵ\epsilon-stochastic-stationary point of problem (1.1). However, these methods require computing a large-batch gradient of size 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) once in every fixed number of iterations and a mini-batch size of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}) at other iterations, similar to their smooth counterparts. Tran-Dinh et al. [38] proposed Hybrid-SGD and showed that it achieves the same 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) complexity for finding an ϵ\epsilon-stochastic-stationary point of problem (1.1), provided that the initial batch size is chosen as 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}). Without this large initial batch, however, Hybrid-SGD can only guarantee a near-optimal 𝒪~​(ϵ−3)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}) complexity. More recently, Xu and Xu [46] proposed ProxSTORM, which incorporates the variance-reduced gradient estimator from STORM [12] to avoid computing large-batch gradients and achieves an SFO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) for finding an ϵ\epsilon-stochastic-stationary point of problem (1.1).

Recently, there has been growing interest in developing stochastic algorithms for tackling problem (1.1) when h≠0h\not=0 and ℳ\mathcal{M} is a compact submanifold of ℰ1\mathcal{E}_{1}. For the setting where 𝒜=ℐ\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{I}, Li et al. [30] proposed a Riemannian stochastic subgradient (RSSG) method when hh is a weakly convex function and showed that it has an iteration complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4}) for driving a certain stationarity measure of problem (1.1) to below ϵ\epsilon. Wang et al. [39] proposed two Riemannian stochastic proximal gradient methods, R-ProxSGD and R-ProxSPB, when hh is a convex function. These two methods are the Riemannian counterparts of the Euclidean proximal SGD [36] and proximal SpiderBoost [40] methods, respectively. To obtain an ϵ\epsilon-RSS point of problem (1.1), R-ProxSGD and R-ProxSPB require 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4}) and 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) SFO calls, respectively. For the setting where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a linear map, Peng et al. [33] proposed a Riemannian stochastic smoothing method when hh is a weakly convex function, which has an SFO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−5)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-5}) for finding a so-called generalized ϵ\epsilon-stationary point of problem (1.1). Using a splitting technique, Deng et al. [13] proposed a stochastic manifold inexact augmented Lagrangian (StoManIAL) framework when hh is a convex function. By employing the Riemannian recursive momentum method as a subroutine, StoManIAL achieves an SFO complexity of 𝒪~​(ϵ−3.5)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3.5}) for finding an ϵ\epsilon-RSS point of problem (1.1). Although R-ProxSPB and StoManIAL achieve good complexity results, both of them are nested-loop algorithms that require solving a subproblem at each iteration. Specifically, R-ProxSPB requires solving each subproblem exactly, while StoManIAL requires either finding an ϵk\epsilon_{k}-RSS point of the AL subproblem (which is difficult to verify) or performing 𝒪⁡(2k)\mathcal{O}(2^{k}) Riemannian stochastic gradient steps (which may result in unnecessary but expensive computation in practice) at the kk-th iteration.

In view of the above developments, it is naturally of interest to develop simple yet efficient single-loop stochastic algorithms for tackling problem (1.1) that achieve the optimal SFO complexity. Very recently, Deng et al. [14] proposed a single-loop Riemannian stochastic smoothing method (RSSM), which makes use of the variance-reduced gradient estimator of RSTORM [16], and showed that it has an SFO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) for finding an ϵ\epsilon-RSS point of problem (1.1). Despite their theoretical guarantees, the numerical performance of smoothing-based methods is highly sensitive to the choices of the smoothing parameter and stepsizes and can be unsatisfactory even in the deterministic setting. Moreover, RSSM employs a Riemannian recursive momentum estimator that combines tangent vectors at different iterates. As such, it requires vector transport operations, which introduces additional computational cost.

1.2 Our Contributions

We summarize the main contributions of this paper as follows.

  • •

    We reformulate problem (1.1) as a Riemannian minimax problem and propose an efficient stochastic Riemannian alternating descent ascent method with recursive momentum (StoRADA-RM) to tackle it. At each iteration, the proposed method performs one or multiple Riemannian stochastic gradient descent steps to approximately minimize a value function associated with the inner maximization problem, followed by a proximal gradient ascent step on a regularized version of the objective function of the minimax problem. Since full gradient information is often inaccessible or too expensive to compute in our setting, we adopt a Euclidean momentum-based variance-reduced gradient estimator that requires only 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) SFO calls per iteration. With such an estimator, our proposed method does not need to perform any vector transport operations, which is in sharp contrast to the method proposed in [14]. Our proposed StoRADA-RM is obtained by adapting our earlier RADA-RGD [44], which is developed for a deterministic setting, to a stochastic setting. Still, even when specialized to the setting where ℳ\mathcal{M} is a closed convex set in a Euclidean space, StoRADA-RM remains new.

  • •

    We establish the convergence of StoRADA-RM and show that both its iteration complexity and SFO complexity for finding an ϵ\epsilon-RSS point of problem (1.1) are 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}). The iteration complexity matches the best known in the literature for deterministic Riemannian nonsmooth composite optimization; see, e.g., [3, 13, 43]. Remarkably, the SFO complexity of StoRADA-RM not only matches the state-of-the-art in the literature for Riemannian nonsmooth composite expectation optimization (see, e.g., [39, 14]) but also attains the optimal lower bound established in [2] for smooth nonconvex optimization with stochastic first-order algorithms. To obtain the said complexity results, we develop new techniques to (i) control the estimation error of the recursive momentum estimator in the presence of a nonsmooth composite term in the objective function, thus extending the results in [28]; and (ii) analyze the progress made at each iteration of our proposed method in the absence of a sufficient decrease property of the iterates generated by the Riemannian stochastic gradient steps, thus bypassing a key requirement in the analysis of RADA-RGD in [44].

  • •

    We present numerical results on sparse PCA and CISE problems to demonstrate the efficiency of our proposed StoRADA-RM. The proposed method consistently returns solutions with lower objective values and has significantly lower computational cost compared with existing state-of-the-art methods, including R-ProxSPB [39], StoManIAL [13], and RSSM [14]. In particular, although both StoRADA-RM and RSSM are single-loop algorithms with the same SFO complexity of 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}), StoRADA-RM is substantially more efficient in practice.

A comparison of existing methods for tackling problem (1.1) is summarized in Table 1.

1.3 Organization

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We first introduce the notation and cover some preliminaries on Riemannian optimization and convex analysis in Section 2. We then present our proposed algorithm in Section 3, followed by its convergence analysis in Section 4. Then, we present numerical results on sparse PCA and CISE to illustrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithms in Section 5. Finally, we draw some conclusions in Section 6.

2 Notation and Preliminaries

We first introduce the notation and some basic concepts in Riemannian optimization [1, 8]. We use ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\,\!\cdot\,,\cdot\rangle and ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| to denote the standard inner product and its induced norm on the Euclidean space ℰ\mathcal{E}, respectively. For a linear map 𝒜:ℰ1→ℰ2\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{E}_{1}\to\mathcal{E}_{2}, its adjoint is denoted by 𝒜⊤:ℰ2→ℰ1\mathcal{A}^{\top}:\mathcal{E}_{2}\to\mathcal{E}_{1}. Then, for a smooth function f:ℰ→ℝf:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and a point x∈ℳx\in\mathcal{M}, the Riemannian gradient of ff at xx is given by grad​f​(x)=projTx​ℳ​(∇f​(x))\mathrm{grad}\,f(x)=\mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{T}_{x}\mathcal{M}}(\nabla f(x)), where proj𝒳​(⋅)\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{X}}(\cdot) is the Euclidean projection operator onto a closed set 𝒳\mathcal{X} and ∇f​(x)\nabla f(x) is the Euclidean gradient of ff at xx. 3 Proposed StoRADA-RM

In this section, we propose an efficient algorithm for tackling the Riemannian nonsmooth expectation optimization problem (1.1).

Main framework

First, we reformulate problem (1.1) as the Riemannian minimax problem

minx∈ℳmaxy∈ℰ2{F(x,y):=f(x)+⟨𝒜(x),y⟩−h∗(y)}.\min_{x\in\mathcal{M}}\,\max_{y\in\mathcal{E}_{2}}\,\left\{F(x,y):=f(x)+\langle\mathcal{A}(x),y\rangle-h^{*}(y)\right\}. (3.1)

In the original formulation (1.1), the composite term h⁡(𝒜⁡(⋅))h(\mathcal{A}(\cdot)) is nonsmooth and nonconvex, which makes the problem difficult to handle directly. By contrast, the reformulation (3.1) decouples the nonsmoothness and nonconvexity: Its objective function is smooth but nonconvex in xx and concave but nonsmooth in yy. One approach to tackling the Riemannian minimax problem (3.1) is to apply the algorithmic framework RADA that we developed in [44]. Specifically, at the kk-th iteration, where k≥1k\geq 1, we approximately solve the following problem to compute the next iterate xk+1x_{k+1}:

minx∈ℳ{Φk(x):=maxy∈ℰ2{F(x,y)−λk2∥y∥2−βk2∥y−yk∥2}}.\min_{x\in\mathcal{M}}\left\{\Phi_{k}(x):=\max_{y\in\mathcal{E}_{2}}\left\{F(x,y)-\frac{\lambda_{k}}{2}\|y\|^{2}-\frac{\beta_{k}}{2}\|y-y_{k}\|^{2}\right\}\right\}. (3.2)

Here, λk>0\lambda_{k}>0 is the regularization parameter, yk∈dom​h∗y_{k}\in\mathrm{dom}\,h^{*} is the proximal center, and βk≥0\beta_{k}\geq 0 is the proximal parameter. We compute the update

yk+1\displaystyle y_{k+1} =arg​maxy∈ℰ2⁡{F⁡(xk+1,y)−λk2​‖y‖2−βk2​‖y−yk‖2}\displaystyle=\argmax_{y\in\mathcal{E}_{2}}\left\{F(x_{k+1},y)-\frac{\lambda_{k}}{2}\|y\|^{2}-\frac{\beta_{k}}{2}\|y-y_{k}\|^{2}\right\} (3.3)
=proxh∗/(λk+βk)​(𝒜⁡(xk+1)+βk​ykλk+βk),\displaystyle=\mathrm{prox}_{{h^{*}/(\lambda_{k}+\beta_{k})}}\left(\frac{\mathcal{A}(x_{k+1})+\beta_{k}y_{k}}{\lambda_{k}+\beta_{k}}\right),

which can be regarded as performing a proximal gradient ascent step on the regularized function F(xk+1,⋅)−λk2∥⋅∥2F(x_{k+1},\cdot)-\frac{\lambda_{k}}{2}\|\cdot\|^{2}.

Riemannian stochastic gradient descent

To approximately solve the subproblem (3.2) for a given k≥1k\geq 1, we leverage the differentiability of value function Φk\Phi_{k}. Specifically, observe that Φk\Phi_{k} can be written as

Φk​(x)=\displaystyle\Phi_{k}(x)= f⁡(x)+M(λk+βk)​h​(𝒜⁡(x)+βk​yk)−βk2​‖yk‖2.\displaystyle f(x)+M_{{(\lambda_{k}+\beta_{k})h}}\left(\mathcal{A}(x)+\beta_{k}y_{k}\right)-\frac{\beta_{k}}{2}\|y_{k}\|^{2}. (3.4)

As shown in [44, Section 3.1], the function Φk\Phi_{k} is differentiable with

∇Φk(x)=∇f(x)+∇𝒜(x)⊤proxh∗/(λk+βk)(𝒜⁡(x)+βk​ykλk+βk),\nabla\Phi_{k}(x)=\nabla f(x)+\nabla\mathcal{A}(x)^{\top}\mathrm{prox}_{{h^{*}}/(\lambda_{k}+\beta_{k})}\left(\frac{\mathcal{A}(x)+\beta_{k}y_{k}}{\lambda_{k}+\beta_{k}}\right), (3.5)

where ∇𝒜\nabla\mathcal{A} denotes the Jacobian of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Unlike in the setting considered in [44], the full gradient ∇f\nabla f in (3.5) is intractable in our current setting. Thus, instead of performing Riemannian gradient steps on the value function Φk\Phi_{k} as in [44, Algorithm 3], we perform Riemannian stochastic gradient steps. Specifically, let T≥1T\geq 1 be the number of Riemannian stochastic gradient steps to be performed on Φk\Phi_{k}. Let xk,1=xkx_{k,1}=x_{k} and xk,tx_{k,t} be the iterate at the tt-th inner iteration for t∈{1,2,…,T}t\in\{1,2,\ldots,T\}. In view of (3.5), we define the Riemannian stochastic gradient of Φk\Phi_{k} at xk,tx_{k,t} as

Dk,tR=projTxk,t​ℳ(dk,t+∇𝒜(xk,t)⊤proxh∗/(λk+βk)(𝒜⁡(xk,t)+βk​ykλk+βk)).D_{k,t}^{R}=\mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{T}_{x_{k,t}}\mathcal{M}}\left(d_{k,t}+\nabla\mathcal{A}(x_{k,t})^{\top}\mathrm{prox}_{{h^{*}}/(\lambda_{k}+\beta_{k})}\left(\frac{\mathcal{A}(x_{k,t})+\beta_{k}y_{k}}{\lambda_{k}+\beta_{k}}\right)\right). (3.6)

Here, dk,td_{k,t} is a stochastic estimator of ∇f​(xk,t)\nabla f(x_{k,t}), which will be specified in (3.8). We then choose a stepsize ζk,t>0\zeta_{k,t}>0 and compute the update

xk,t+1=Rxk,t​(−ζk,t​Dk,tR)x_{k,t+1}=\mathrm{R}_{x_{k,t}}(-\zeta_{k,t}D_{k,t}^{R}) (3.7)

for t=1,2,…,Tt=1,2,\ldots,T to obtain xk+1=xk+1,1=xk,T+1x_{k+1}=x_{k+1,1}=x_{k,T+1}.

Recursive momentum estimator

To construct the stochastic estimator dk,td_{k,t} for t=1,2,…,Tt=1,2,\ldots,T, we adopt the recursive momentum approach proposed in [12, 28]. The approach relies on the following standard assumption.

Assumption 3.1.

The function ff is equipped with an SFO, which is a map that, when queried at the point x∈ℳx\in\mathcal{M}, returns an unbiased estimate f⁡(x,θ)f(x;\theta) of the function value f⁡(x)f(x) and an unbiased estimate ∇f​(x,θ)\nabla f(x;\theta) of the gradient ∇f​(x)\nabla f(x).

Given the initial stochastic estimator dk,1d_{k,1} of ∇f​(xk,1)\nabla f(x_{k,1}), the stochastic estimator dk,t+1d_{k,t+1} for t=1,2,…,Tt=1,2,\ldots,T is constructed via

dk,t+1=∇fSk,t+1​(xk,t+1)+(1−αk,t)​(dk,t−∇fSk,t+1​(xk,t)).d_{k,t+1}=\nabla f_{S_{k,t+1}}(x_{k,t+1})+(1-\alpha_{k,t})(d_{k,t}-\nabla f_{S_{k,t+1}}(x_{k,t})). (3.8)

Here, αk,t∈(0,1]\alpha_{k,t}\in(0,1] is a given weight and Sk,t+1S_{k,t+1} is a sampling set of size |Sk,t+1|=b|S_{k,t+1}|=b, where b≥1b\geq 1 is given. We assume that the initial sampling set S1S_{1} and the mini-batches {Sk,t+1∣k≥1,1≤t≤T}\{S_{k,t+1}\mid k\geq 1,1\leq t\leq T\} are mutually independent. By convention, we set dk,T+1=dk+1,1d_{k,T+1}=d_{k+1,1}.

Choice of parameters

To obtain an efficient instantiation of the above algorithmic framework, we need to choose the parameters {λk}\{\lambda_{k}\}, {βk}\{\beta_{k}\}, {αk,t}\{\alpha_{k,t}\}, and {ζk,t}\{\zeta_{k,t}\} judiciously, so as to simultaneously control the errors of the stochastic estimators {dk,t}\{d_{k,t}\} and ensure sufficient progress towards stationarity is made when the value functions {Φk}\{\Phi_{k}\} in successive iterations are approximately minimized. First, for k≥1k\geq 1 and t=1,2,…,Tt=1,2,\ldots,T, we set the momentum weight αk,t\alpha_{k,t} and stepsize ζk,t\zeta_{k,t} as

αk,t=((k−1)T+t)−2/3\alpha_{k,t}=((k-1)T+t)^{-2/3} (3.9)

and

ζk,t=ξkαk,t1/3(δ0+∑i=1k−1∑j=1T∥Di,jR∥2+∑j=1t∥Dk,jR∥2)−1/3,\zeta_{k,t}=\xi_{k}\alpha_{k,t}^{1/3}\left({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\delta_{0}+}}}\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\sum_{j=1}^{T}\|D_{i,j}^{R}\|^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{t}\|D_{k,j}^{R}\|^{2}\right)^{-1/3}, (3.10)

respectively, where δ0>0\delta_{0}>0 and ξk∈[ξmin,ξk−1]\xi_{k}\in[\xi_{\min},\xi_{k-1}] with ξ0≥ξmin>0\xi_{0}\geq\xi_{\min}>0 to ensure that the stepsize is nonzero even when all the Riemannian stochastic gradients are zero. These choices are motivated by the parameter balancing mechanism in STORM+ [28, 14]. The underlying idea is to coordinate the use of past gradient information with the movement of the iterates. On one hand, the momentum weight αk,t\alpha_{k,t} is used to induce a variance reduction effect through the correction term (1−αk,t)​(dk,t−∇fSk,t+1​(xk,t))(1-\alpha_{k,t})(d_{k,t}-\nabla f_{S_{k,t+1}}(x_{k,t})) in (3.8); cf. [28]. To accommodate the TT inner updates in StoRADA-RM, we index αk,t\alpha_{k,t} by the total number of inner updates, i.e., (k−1)​T+t(k-1)T+t. On the other hand, the stepsize ζk,t\zeta_{k,t} uses the momentum weight αk,t\alpha_{k,t} and the Riemannian stochastic gradients {Dk′,t′R}\{D_{k^{\prime},t^{\prime}}^{R}\} computed so far to control the progress made between two successive outer iterations.

Next, let λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0, β1≥0\beta_{1}\geq 0, and ρ>1\rho>1 be fixed. For k≥1k\geq 1, we set the regularization parameter λk\lambda_{k} and the proximal parameter βk\beta_{k} in the subproblem (3.2) as

λk=λ1k1/3and0≤βk≤β1(k)ρ,\lambda_{k}=\frac{\lambda_{1}}{k^{1/3}}\quad\mbox{and}\quad 0\leq\beta_{k}\leq\frac{\beta_{1}}{(k)^{\rho}}, (3.11)

respectively. Unlike in the deterministic setting considered in [44], where {λk}\{\lambda_{k}\} is chosen to be a constant sequence, we choose a decreasing sequence {λk}\{\lambda_{k}\} whose rate of decay is compatible with that of {ζk,t}\{\zeta_{k,t}\}. Moreover, we impose a summability condition on {βk}\{\beta_{k}\}. These choices allow us to bound the accumulated change in values of the different value functions that arise in the course of our proposed method and show that in expectation, both the norm of the Riemannian gradient of the value function and the regularization error decay at the same rate; see Theorem 11.

The proposed StoRADA-RM method is formally presented in Algorithm 1.

Several remarks on StoRADA-RM are in order. First, although the method is a natural instantiation of the RADA framework in the stochastic setting, the use of the recursive momentum estimator only yields an approximation of the full gradient of the value function. The approximation error at each inner iteration accumulates, which leads to difficulty in establishing the sufficient decrease property needed in the analysis of RADA (see [44, displayed eqn. (13)]). To circumvent this difficulty, we need to choose the momentum weights, the stepsizes, and the regularization parameters carefully so that the gradient estimation errors and the progress made between two successive outer iterations can be controlled simultaneously. This presents a significant challenge in the analysis of StoRADA-RM that is not seen in the analyses of RADA [44] and the recursive momentum estimator-based methods in [12, 28].

Second, StoRADA-RM is simple to implement while retaining the optimal SFO complexity. It can be regarded as a single-loop method since TT is fixed (and can even be set to one). By contrast, the stochastic Riemannian AL method in [13] requires solving a subproblem either to ϵk\epsilon_{k}-stochastic stationarity or by performing 𝒪⁡(2k)\mathcal{O}(2^{k}) inner updates at the kk-th iteration, both of which are computationally prohibitive. On the other hand, the batch size bb in StoRADA-RM can be taken as 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1). This makes StoRADA-RM easier to implement and potentially more efficient than R-ProxSPB [39], as the latter requires computing the full gradient or a large-batch gradient of size 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}) once in every fixed number of iterations. Moreover, the stepsizes {ζk,t}\{\zeta_{k,t}\} are independent of the problem parameters, such as the Lipschitz constant of ∇f\nabla f. This makes the stepsize scheme of StoRADA-RM more flexible than those of not only the stochastic R-ProxSPB [39] and StoManIAL [13] but also the deterministic RADA-RGD [44].

Finally, we compare StoRADA-RM with the recently proposed RSSM [14], which is also single-loop and employs the recursive momentum estimator. Specifically, RSSM performs a single Riemannian stochastic gradient step to approximately solve the smoothed subproblem

minx∈ℳ⁡{f⁡(x)+Mλk​h​(𝒜⁡(x))},\min_{x\in\mathcal{M}}\left\{f(x)+M_{\lambda_{k}h}(\mathcal{A}(x))\right\},

which can be viewed as a special case of our subproblem (3.2) with βk≡0\beta_{k}\equiv 0 for all k≥1k\geq 1. Despite this connection, the two methods differ fundamentally in their design philosophies. StoRADA-RM exploits the intrinsic minimax structure of the original problem to decouple the nonsmoothness and nonconvexity. Moreover, it allows multiple Riemannian stochastic gradient steps. Although such a flexibility complicates the convergence analysis of the method, it yields more accurate solutions to the subproblems and contributes to the favorable numerical performance of the method; see Section 5. Lastly, StoRADA-RM adopts the Euclidean recursive momentum estimator (3.8), which, unlike RSSM, avoids the need to perform vector transport operations, thereby further improving its computational efficiency.

4 Complexity Analysis of StoRADA-RM

In this section, we study the convergence behavior of StoRADA-RM (Algorithm 1).

4.1 Assumptions and Useful Lemmas

We begin with the assumptions used in our analysis.

Assumption 4.1.

The manifold ℳ⊆ℰ1\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{1} is compact.

Assumption 4.2.
  • (i)

    The function f:ℰ1→ℝf:\mathcal{E}_{1}\to\mathbb{R} is continuously differentiable and satisfies the descent property

    f⁡(x′)≤f⁡(x)+⟨∇f​(x),x′−x⟩+Lf2​‖x′−x‖2,∀x,x′∈ℳ.f(x^{\prime})\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),\,x^{\prime}-x\rangle+\frac{L_{f}}{2}\|x^{\prime}-x\|^{2},\quad\forall\,x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}.
  • (ii)

    The map 𝒜:ℰ1→ℰ2\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{E}_{1}\to\mathcal{E}_{2} and its Jacobian ∇𝒜\nabla\mathcal{A} are L𝒜0L_{\mathcal{A}}^{0}-Lipschitz and L𝒜1L_{\mathcal{A}}^{1}-Lipschitz over conv​ℳ\mathrm{conv}\,\mathcal{M}, respectively. In other words, for any x,x′∈conv​ℳx,x^{\prime}\in\mathrm{conv}\,\mathcal{M}, we have

    ‖𝒜⁡(x)−𝒜⁡(x′)‖≤L𝒜0​‖x−x′‖,\displaystyle\|\mathcal{A}(x)-\mathcal{A}(x^{\prime})\|\leq L_{\mathcal{A}}^{0}\|x-x^{\prime}\|,
    ‖∇𝒜​(x)−∇𝒜​(x′)‖≤L𝒜1​‖x−x′‖.\displaystyle\|\nabla\mathcal{A}(x)-\nabla\mathcal{A}(x^{\prime})\|\leq L_{\mathcal{A}}^{1}\|x-x^{\prime}\|.

    Moreover, the Jacobian ∇𝒜\nabla\mathcal{A} is bounded over conv​ℳ\mathrm{conv}\,\mathcal{M}, i.e.,

    ρ𝒜:=supx∈conv​ℳ‖∇𝒜​(x)‖<+∞.\rho_{\mathcal{A}}:=\sup_{x\,\in\,\mathrm{conv}\,\mathcal{M}}\,\|\nabla\mathcal{A}(x)\|<+\infty.

Assumption 4.3.

The unbiased gradient estimate ∇f​(x,θ)\nabla f(x;\theta) has bounded variance and satisfies a so-called mean-squared smoothness property, i.e., there exist σ>0\sigma>0 and L~f>0\tilde{L}_{f}>0 such that for all x,x′∈ℳx,\,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}, we have

𝔼ω∼𝒟​[∇f​(x,ω)]=∇f​(x),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\omega\sim\mathcal{D}}[\nabla f(x;\omega)]=\nabla f(x), (4.2)
𝔼ω∼𝒟​[‖∇f​(x,ω)−∇f​(x)‖2]≤σ2,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\omega\sim\mathcal{D}}[\|\nabla f(x;\omega)-\nabla f(x)\|^{2}]\leq\sigma^{2}, (4.3)
𝔼ω∼𝒟​[‖∇f​(x,ω)−∇f​(x′,ω)‖2]≤L~f2​‖x−x′‖2.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\omega\sim\mathcal{D}}[\|\nabla f(x;\omega)-\nabla f(x^{\prime};\omega)\|^{2}]\leq\tilde{L}_{f}^{2}\|x-x^{\prime}\|^{2}.\quad (4.4)

Assumptions 4.1 and 4.2 are standard in the context of Riemannian nonsmooth composite optimization; see, e.g., [10, 9, 21, 22, 43, 14]. Assumption 4.3 is standard in the context of Riemannian stochastic optimization; see, e.g., [16, 14, 39, 46].

The following lemma, which is extracted from [7, Appendix B], shows that the retraction satisfies first- and second-order boundedness conditions on ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Suppose that Assumption 4.1 holds. Then, there exist κ1,κ2>0\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2}>0 such that

‖Rx​(v)−x‖≤κ1​‖v‖and‖Rx​(v)−x−v‖≤κ2​‖v‖2\|\mathrm{R}_{x}(v)-x\|\leq\kappa_{1}\|v\|\quad\text{{and}}\quad\|\mathrm{R}_{x}(v)-x-v\|\leq\kappa_{2}\|v\|^{2}

4.3 Bound on Υe\Upsilon_{e}

4.4 Complexity Bounds

Our goal now is to derive the iteration complexity and SFO complexity of Algorithm 1 for computing an approximate Riemannian-stochastic-stationary point of problem (1.1), which is defined as follows.

Definition 10.

Given ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the point x∈ℳx\in\mathcal{M} is an ϵ\epsilon-Riemannian-stochastic-stationary (ϵ\epsilon-RSS) point of problem (1.1) if there exists a point p∈ℰ2p\in\mathcal{E}_{2} such that

max{𝔼[dist(0,gradf(x)+projTx​ℳ(∇𝒜(x)⊤∂h(p)))],𝔼[‖p−𝒜(x)‖]}≤ϵ,\max\!\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{dist}\left(0,\,\mathrm{grad}\,f(x)+\mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{T}_{x}\mathcal{M}}\left(\nabla\mathcal{A}(x)^{\top}\partial h(p)\right)\right)\right],\,\mathbb{E}[\left\|p-\mathcal{A}(x)\right\|]\right\}\leq\epsilon,

where the expectation 𝔼⁡[⋅]\mathbb{E}[\cdot] is taken over all randomness in the course of generating xx.

We remark that the above stationarity notion is generalized from those introduced in [13, 3, 29] for deterministic settings.

With the above preparations, we are ready to prove the main result of this paper.

Suppose that Assumptions 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3 hold. Given ϵ>0\epsilon>0, let {xk}\{x_{k}\} be the sequence generated by Algorithm 1. Since Algorithm 1 only requires 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) SFO calls at each iteration, the total number of SFO calls is also 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}).  

Theorem 11 shows that both the iteration complexity and SFO complexity of the proposed StoRADA-RM are 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}). It is worth noting that the iteration complexity coincides with the best known in the literature for deterministic Riemannian nonsmooth composite optimization (see, e.g., [3, 13, 43]), while the SFO complexity not only matches the best known for Riemannian nonsmooth composite expectation optimization (see, e.g., [14, 39]) but also attains the optimal lower bound established in [2] for smooth nonconvex optimization with stochastic first-order algorithms under the mean-squared smoothness assumption (4.4).

It is also worth emphasizing that the strategy for establishing the iteration complexity of the proposed StoRADA-RM is significantly different from that for its deterministic counterpart RADA-RGD [44]. In particular, the sufficient decrease property that is central to the complexity analysis of RADA no longer holds due to gradient estimation errors, which accumulate across the inner iterations of StoRADA-RM. To address this challenge, we characterize the impact of the accumulated gradient estimation errors on the progress made by StoRADA-RM towards stationarity. Furthermore, our analysis allows for considerable flexibility in the choice of stepsizes {ζk,t}\{\zeta_{k,t}\}. Unlike RADA-RGD, where {ζk,t}\{\zeta_{k,t}\} must satisfy a line-search condition requiring extra objective function evaluations, StoRADA-RM avoids this cost while preserving the same iteration complexity guarantee.

5 Numerical Results

In this section, we report numerical results of our proposed StoRADA-RM for solving sparse PCA and CISE problems. The corresponding experiments were implemented in MATLAB 2023b and evaluated on Apple M2 Pro CPU.

We begin by specifying the default parameter settings used in our experiments. For StoRADA-RM, we adopt the update scheme for {βk}\{\beta_{k}\} from RADA-RGD [44] to improve practical performance. Given constants τ1∈(0,1)\tau_{1}\in(0,1) and τ2∈(0,1)\tau_{2}\in(0,1), we set

βk+1=β1(k+1)(k+1)ρwithβ1(k+1)={τ2​β1(k),if ​δk+1≥τ1​δk;β1(k),if ​δk+1<τ1​δk,\beta_{k+1}=\frac{\beta_{1}^{(k+1)}}{(k+1)^{\rho}}\quad\mbox{with}\quad\beta_{1}^{(k+1)}=\left\{\begin{aligned} \tau_{2}\beta_{1}^{(k)},&\quad\text{if }\delta_{k+1}\geq\tau_{1}\delta_{k};\\ \beta_{1}^{(k)},&\quad\text{if }\delta_{k+1}<\tau_{1}\delta_{k},\end{aligned}\right. (5.1)

for k≥1k\geq 1, where β1(1)=β1\beta_{1}^{(1)}=\beta_{1} and δk+1\delta_{k+1} is defined as

δk+1:=‖(λk+βk)​yk+1−βk​yk‖∞,∀k≥0.{\delta_{k+1}}:=\|(\lambda_{k}+\beta_{k})y_{k+1}-\beta_{k}y_{k}\|_{\infty},\quad\forall\,k\geq 0. (5.2)

Here, we adopt the convention that λ0=λ1\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{1}, β0=β1\beta_{0}=\beta_{1}, and y0=y1y_{0}=y_{1} when computing δ1\delta_{1}. For our tests, we set ρ=1.5\rho=1.5, τ1=0.999\tau_{1}=0.999, and τ2=0.9\tau_{2}=0.9. We initialize λ1=10−6\lambda_{1}=10^{-6} and use λk=λ1k−1/3\lambda_{k}=\lambda_{1}k^{-1/3} for k≥2k\geq 2. We choose ξk=max⁡{ξ0/k1/2,0.01}\xi_{k}=\max\{\xi_{0}/k^{1/2},0.01\} for k≥1k\geq 1, where ξ0\xi_{0} is tuned for each application problem. We adopt the same smoothing parameters {λk}\{\lambda_{k}\} and stepsizes {ζk}\{\zeta_{k}\} for RSSM [14] to improve its practical performance. For StoManIAL, we set the penalty parameter of the AL function as σk=1000⋅22​k/7\sigma_{k}=1000\cdot 2^{2k/7}, the dual stepsize as

βk=1000​min⁡{‖𝒜⁡(x1)−y1‖​log2​2‖𝒜⁡(xk+1)−yk+1‖​(k+1)2​log⁡(k+2),1},\beta_{k}=1000\min\left\{\frac{\|\mathcal{A}(x_{1})-y_{1}\|\log^{2}2}{\|\mathcal{A}(x_{k+1})-y_{k+1}\|(k+1)^{2}\log(k+2)},1\right\},

and the maximum number of inner iterations as Tk=min⁡{2k,5000}T_{k}=\min\{2^{k},5000\}, where k≥1k\geq 1. Compared with the original settings σk=22​k/7\sigma_{k}=2^{2k/7} and Tk=2kT_{k}=2^{k} of StoManIAL [13], introducing the coefficient 1000 enables StoManIAL to generate sparser solutions in fewer iterations, while the cap 5000 prevents the algorithm from taking too much time in one outer iteration, especially when kk is large. Finally, we terminate StoRADA-RM, StoManIAL, and R-ProxSPB when ‖xk+1−xk‖≤tol1\|x_{k+1}-x_{k}\|\leq\text{tol}_{1} with tol1>0\text{tol}_{1}>0. Note that these three algorithms all perform multiple Riemannian stochastic gradient steps to generate xk+1x_{k+1}, while RSSM only performs a single such step. Thus, the gap ‖xk+1−xk‖\|x_{k+1}-x_{k}\| generated by the former can be relatively larger than the latter. To ensure fairness in comparison, we terminate RSSM when ‖xk+1−xk‖≤tol2\|x_{k+1}-x_{k}\|\leq\text{tol}_{2} with tol2<tol1\text{tol}_{2}<\text{tol}_{1}.

5.1 Sparse PCA

In this subsection, we compare the proposed StoRADA-RM with RSSM [14], R-ProxSPB [39], and StoManIAL [13] on the sparse PCA problem.

Let a∈ℝda\in\mathbb{R}^{d} represent a random data point following a certain distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}. To achieve a good balance between dimension reduction and interpretability, sparse PCA seeks principal components with few nonzero components. This motivates the following formulation of sparse PCA [24]:

minX∈𝒮⁡(d,r)⁡{𝔼a∼𝒟​[‖a−X​X⊤​a‖2]+μ​‖X‖1}.\min_{X\in\mathcal{S}(d,r)}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\mathcal{D}}[\|a-XX^{\top}a\|^{2}]+\mu\|X\|_{1}\right\}. (5.3)

Here, 𝒮⁡(d,r)={X∈ℝd×r∣X⊤​X=Ir}\mathcal{S}(d,r)=\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\mid X^{\top}X=I_{r}\} is the Stiefel manifold with IrI_{r} being the rr-by-rr identity matrix, μ>0\mu>0 is the weighting parameter, and ‖X‖1=∑i,j|Xi​j|\|X\|_{1}=\sum_{i,j}|X_{ij}| is the ℓ1\ell_{1}-norm of the matrix XX. When the support Ω={a1,a2,…,aN}\Omega=\{a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{N}\} is finite and aa is uniformly distributed on Ω\Omega, the expectation term 𝔼a∼𝒟​[‖a−X​X⊤​a‖2]\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\mathcal{D}}[\|a-XX^{\top}a\|^{2}] reduces to the finite-sum 1N​∑i=1N‖ai−X​X⊤​ai‖2\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|a_{i}-XX^{\top}a_{i}\|^{2}.

We first consider the finite-sum case of problem (5.3) and perform tests on synthetic datasets and the real dataset coil-100 [32], which contains 7200 image samples of 100 objects taken from different angles with d=1024d=1024. For the synthetic data, we generate the data matrix A=[a1,a2,…,aN]A=[a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{N}] with N=10000N=10000 and d∈{400,600,800,1000}d\in\{400,600,800,1000\} as in [51]. For StoRADA-RM, we set β1=1\beta_{1}=1, T=10T=10, ξ0=1\xi_{0}=1, and δ0=1\delta_{0}=1. For the inner subproblem solver of StoManIAL, we fine-tuned the parameters and found the following settings worked well in our tests:

ζk,t=ζk(1+∑i=1t∑a∈Sk,i∥gradℒk(xk,i;a)∥/b)−1/3,ζk=0.05⋅2−k/3,\zeta_{k,t}={\zeta_{k}}{\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{t}\sum_{a\in S_{k,i}}\|\mathrm{grad}\,\mathcal{L}_{k}(x_{k,i};a)\|/b\right)^{-{1}/{3}}},\quad\zeta_{k}={0.05}\cdot{2^{-{k}/{3}}}, (5.4)

and αk,t=100​ζk,t2/k1/2\alpha_{k,t}=100\zeta_{k,t}^{2}/k^{1/2}, where k≥1k\geq 1 and t=1,2,…,Tt=1,2,\ldots,T. For R-ProxSPB, we set γ=1/Lf\gamma=1/{L}_{f} and η=0.1\eta=0.1 after fine-tuning to enhance its practical performance. Note that these values violate the theoretical requirements of R-ProxSPB, where γ\gamma is required to be 0.4 and η\eta depends on problem-specific parameters, κ2\kappa_{2}, LhL_{h}, and a uniform Hessian bound for ff. We set the batch size b=100b=100 for StoRADA-RM, StoManIAL, and RSSM. For R-ProxSPB, we set the large-batch size to NN in every 100 iterations and use a small-batch size of 100 in the other iterations. For the stopping criteria, we set tol1=10−3\text{tol}_{1}=10^{-3} and tol2=0.2​tol1\text{tol}_{2}=0.2\text{tol}_{1}.

The average results of 20 runs with different data matrices and initial points are presented in Table 2, where Φ\Phi denotes the objective value of problem (5.3), “cpu” represents the cpu time in seconds, and “iter” denotes the outer iteration number. We also compare the reconstruction loss value (denoted by “loss”), defined as 1N​∑i=1N‖ai−X​X⊤​ai‖2\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|a_{i}-XX^{\top}a_{i}\|^{2}, and the sparsity of XX (denoted by “spar”), measured as the percentage of entries with absolute value less than 10−510^{-5}. From Table 2, we observe that the proposed single-loop StoRADA-RM algorithm always returns the best solutions in terms of the objective value Φ\Phi and is the most efficient among the compared algorithms. In particular, although both StoRADA-RM and RSSM are single-loop algorithms with the same optimal SFO complexity, the former produces solutions with higher sparsity and lower reconstruction loss and does so in significantly less time. The superior performance stems from its ability to perform multiple Riemannian stochastic gradient steps when solving the subproblems, thereby yielding more accurate xx-updates and substantially reducing the number of outer iterations. Moreover, when compared with the two nested-loop algorithms StoManIAL and R-ProxSPB, the efficiency of StoRADA-RM becomes even more pronounced, particularly in high-dimensional settings with large dd and rr.

Next, we consider the general case of problem (5.3), where the data point aa is randomly generated at each update. Specifically, we first generate an auxiliary dataset {ai}i=1N0\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{0}} with N0=200N_{0}=200, following the same procedure used for the finite-sum case, and set

a¯=1N0​∑i=1N0ai,andΣ=1N0−1​∑i=1N0(ai−a¯)​(ai−a¯)⊤+10−6​Id.\bar{a}=\frac{1}{N_{0}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{0}}a_{i},\quad\text{and}\quad\Sigma=\frac{1}{N_{0}-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{0}}(a_{i}-\bar{a})(a_{i}-\bar{a})^{\top}+10^{-6}I_{d}.

At each stochastic gradient evaluation, the required data samples are then drawn independently from 𝒩⁡(𝟎,Σ)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\Sigma). For R-ProxSPB, we set the large-batch size to 4000040000 in every 200 iterations and use a small-batch size of 200 in the other iterations. All compared algorithms are executed for 20 seconds, and the other parameter settings remain the same as in the finite-sum case. We plot the objective value Φ\Phi against the runtime for two representative instances in Figure 1. As shown in the figure, our proposed StoRADA-RM reduces the objective value significantly faster than the other compared algorithms and can find the best solution in terms of the objective value.

5.2 Results on CISE

In this subsection, we compare the proposed StoRADA-RM with RSSM [14], R-ProxSPB [39], and StoManIAL [13] on the CISE problem. The CISE problem, which aims at simultaneously achieving sparse sufficient dimension reduction and screening out irrelevant and redundant variables efficiently, admits the following formulation [11]:

minX∈𝒮⁡(d,r)⁡{𝔼a∼𝒟​[‖a−X​X⊤​a‖2]+μ^​‖X‖2,1}.\min_{X\in\mathcal{S}(d,r)}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\mathcal{D}}[\|a-XX^{\top}a\|^{2}]+\hat{\mu}\|X\|_{2,1}\right\}. (5.5)

Here, ‖X‖2,1:=∑i=1d∑j=1rXi​j2\|X\|_{2,1}:=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{r}X_{ij}^{2}} is the ℓ2,1\ell_{2,1}-norm of the matrix XX, which can shrink the corresponding row vectors of irrelevant variables to zero. We set μ^=μ​r+ln⁡(d)\hat{\mu}=\mu\sqrt{r+\ln(d)} as [42], where the constant μ>0\mu>0 controls the sparsity.

We consider both the finite-sum and general cases of problem (5.5) as in Section 5.1 and conduct experiments following the setup therein. For StoRADA-RM, we set T=50T=50 and ξ0=0.5\xi_{0}=0.5. For the inner subproblem solver of StoManIAL, namely RSTORM, we fine-tuned the parameters and adopted the scheme (5.4) with ζk=0.5⋅2−k/3\zeta_{k}=0.5\cdot 2^{-k/3}. For R-ProxSPB, we set η=0.2\eta=0.2 after careful tuning. For the finite-sum case, the stopping criteria are set as tol1=10−3\text{tol}_{1}=10^{-3} and tol2=0.4​tol1\text{tol}_{2}=0.4\text{tol}_{1}. The other parameter settings are identical to those in Section 5.1. The average results of 20 runs with different data matrices and initial points for the finite-sum case are presented in Table 3, where “spar” is now defined as the percentage of rows with the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm less than 10−510^{-5}. From Table 3, we see that our proposed StoRADA-RM consistently returns the best solutions in terms of the objective value Φ\Phi while requiring the least computational time. In particular, StoRADA-RM and R-ProxSPB can obtain solutions with similar sparsity level and loss value, while RSSM has difficulty producing a sparse solution. We also plot the objective value Φ\Phi against the runtime for two representative instances of the general case in Figure 2. As illustrated in the figure, our proposed StoRADA-RM is still the most efficient in reducing the objective value Φ\Phi.

6 Concluding Remarks

In this paper, we proposed an efficient algorithm called StoRADA-RM to tackle a class of Riemannian nonsmooth composite expectation optimization problems. Our proposed method exploits the intrinsic minimax structure of these problems by performing one or multiple Riemannian stochastic gradient descent steps and then a proximal gradient ascent step at each iteration. To compute the Riemannian stochastic gradient, we proposed a vector transport-free recursive momentum estimator that requires only 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) SFO calls at each iteration. Theoretically, we proved that both the iteration complexity and SFO complexity of StoRADA-RM for finding an ϵ\epsilon-RSS point of a given problem in the said class are 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}), which is the best known in the literature. The SFO complexity bound also matches the optimal lower bound for smooth nonconvex optimization with stochastic first-order algorithms. Computationally, we presented numerical results on sparse PCA and CISE to demonstrate the superiority of StoRADA-RM over existing state-of-the-art algorithms. An interesting direction for future work is to extend the proposed algorithm to handle the setting where ff is also nonsmooth.
